ABBV-295: AbbVie's Monthly-Dosed Amylin Analog Enters Phase 2 for Obesity — Research Dossier

Medical Disclaimer: Research compounds discussed for educational purposes. Not FDA-approved for human use where applicable. Consult a healthcare provider before use.

What Is ABBV-295?

ABBV-295 is an investigational long-acting amylin analog being developed by AbbVie in collaboration with Gubra, a Danish biotechnology company (Gubra development code: GUB-014295). The compound was discovered using Gubra's streaMLine platform — a proprietary peptide engineering technology designed to extend the duration of action of peptide hormones. AbbVie licensed global development and commercialization rights from Gubra in March 2025.

ABBV-295 belongs to the amylin receptor agonist class — the same mechanistic category as cagrilintide (Novo Nordisk) and eloralintide (Eli Lilly). What distinguishes ABBV-295 within this class is its half-life of approximately 11 to 12 days, the longest published for any amylin analog in human studies. This extended duration underpins AbbVie's Phase 2 investigation of biweekly and monthly dosing — an interval not tested by any other amylin-class compound in development.

Mechanism of Action

ABBV-295 activates amylin receptors (AMY1R, AMY2R, AMY3R) and the calcitonin receptor (CTR). These receptors are distinct from the GLP-1 receptor (the target of semaglutide and liraglutide) and the GIP receptor (co-targeted by tirzepatide). Amylin receptors are heterodimers of CTR paired with receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMPs), and they are concentrated in the area postrema (AP) and nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) of the brainstem — a satiety circuit that operates independently of the GLP-1-targeted arcuate hypothalamus.

Physiological effects of amylin receptor agonism include:

  • Central appetite suppression via brainstem satiety circuits
  • Slowing of gastric emptying, independent of GLP-1 receptor signaling
  • Suppression of postprandial glucagon secretion
  • Modulation of glucose homeostasis through non-insulin-dependent mechanisms

Because amylin and GLP-1 target distinct neural circuits, their effects are additive rather than redundant — the mechanistic rationale for combination programs like CagriSema (cagrilintide + semaglutide) and EloraTZP (eloralintide + tirzepatide). ABBV-295 is currently being evaluated as a monotherapy, though combination potential exists.

Key Research Findings

Phase 1 — Multiple Ascending Dose (MAD) Study

AbbVie presented detailed Phase 1 MAD data at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD 2026, Barcelona, September 30, 2026). The study was conducted in Parts 2B/2C and enrolled 60 participants.

  • Weight loss: Up to 9.8% mean body weight reduction after 12–13 weeks of once-weekly dosing vs. 0.3% placebo (approximately 9.5% placebo-adjusted). The highest dose group drove this figure.
  • Half-life: Approximately 11–12 days — longer than cagrilintide (~7 days) and eloralintide (~7 days). This is the pharmacokinetic basis for less-frequent dosing.
  • Tolerability: Nausea: 33.3% (ABBV-295) vs. 20.0% (placebo). Diarrhea: 20.0% vs. 0.0%. No treatment-related serious adverse events. This GI profile is consistent with other amylin class agents.
  • Limitation: Participants were predominantly male (88%) with mean BMI below 30 kg/m² — not representative of the target Phase 2 population with obesity.

Phase 2 — Dose-Finding Trial (NCT07752979)

Gubra announced Phase 2 initiation in August 2026, triggering a USD 50 million milestone payment. ClinicalTrials.gov listing confirms: start date August 4, 2026.

  • Title: A Phase 2 Dose-Finding Study to Assess the Safety and Efficacy of ABBV-295 in Adults With Obesity or Overweight With Weight-Related Comorbidities
  • Design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled
  • Enrollment: N=360, United States
  • Treatment duration: 52 weeks
  • Primary endpoint: Percentage change in body weight from baseline to week 32
  • Dosing arms: 4 mg weekly, 6 mg weekly, 14 mg weekly, 14 mg every 2 weeks, 8 mg monthly

The Phase 2 design is notable for simultaneously testing three dosing frequencies (weekly, biweekly, monthly) — an unusual breadth for a single Phase 2 trial that reflects AbbVie's strategic interest in the monthly dosing interval as a potential commercial differentiator.

Dosing in Research

In the Phase 1 MAD study: once-weekly subcutaneous injection, doses not publicly specified per cohort. Phase 2 arms: 4 mg weekly, 6 mg weekly, 14 mg weekly, 14 mg every 2 weeks, and 8 mg monthly. All routes are subcutaneous (SC) injection. ABBV-295 is not available outside of clinical trials. Dosing information is provided for research context only and does not constitute medical advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

How is ABBV-295 different from cagrilintide and eloralintide?

All three are long-acting amylin receptor agonists for obesity, but they differ in half-life, dosing interval, and development stage. Cagrilintide (Novo Nordisk) has a ~7-day half-life, is once-weekly, and is in the most advanced regulatory position (FDA NDA under review as CagriSema). Eloralintide (Lilly) is also once-weekly with Phase 3 ENLIGHTEN trials launched in 2026 showing up to 20.1% Phase 2 weight loss at 48 weeks. ABBV-295 (AbbVie/Gubra) has the longest half-life (~11–12 days), enabling investigation of biweekly and monthly dosing — which no other amylin analog is testing. Phase 2 efficacy data are needed before clinical comparisons can be drawn.

What weight loss results did ABBV-295 achieve in Phase 1?

Up to 9.8% mean body weight reduction after 12–13 weeks (placebo-adjusted ~9.5%) in the Phase 1 MAD study. Important caveat: this cohort was predominantly male (88%) with a mean BMI below 30 kg/m², which likely underestimates the drug's efficacy in the target obese population where higher BMI at baseline typically correlates with greater absolute weight loss. Phase 2 results at week 32 (primary endpoint) will be the first adequate efficacy data.

Why would monthly dosing matter for an obesity drug?

Weekly injectable GLP-1-class drugs require 52 injections per year. Monthly dosing would reduce this to 12 injections per year — a potential convenience and adherence advantage, particularly for people who are needle-averse or find weekly self-injection burdensome. If ABBV-295 achieves comparable efficacy at monthly dosing, it would have a differentiated commercial profile versus all other amylin analogs currently in development.

Research Limitations

  • Phase 1 cohort was predominantly male (88%) with low mean BMI (<30), limiting generalizability to obese populations.
  • No Phase 2 efficacy data are available as of November 2026. Phase 2 primary endpoint (week 32) results are not expected until 2027 at earliest.
  • No head-to-head comparison with cagrilintide or eloralintide in human trials.
  • Long-term safety (cardiovascular outcomes, pancreatitis risk, calcitonin effects) has not been evaluated.
  • Peptide sequence not publicly disclosed as of this dossier.

Disclaimer

ABBV-295 is an investigational compound. It is not approved by the FDA or any regulatory authority worldwide for any indication as of November 2026.
